source.title: AegisLLM: Scaling Agentic Systems for Self-Reflective Defense in LLM Security
source.authors: Zi-Kui Cai; Shayan Shabihi; Bang An; Zora Che; B. Bartoldson; B. Kailkhura; Tom Goldstein; Furong Huang

page_placements.theme: Inference-time, gated or by-design reversible methods reach unlearning scores with weights unchanged

record.file_problem: Full paper and appendices are present. There are minor OCR/encoding artifacts, but they do not prevent extraction.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates an alternative, inference-time multi-agent approach on WMDP and reports targeted-knowledge accuracy and general-capability results. It does not test whether recovery attacks work.
record.gate_note: The WMDP accuracy, MMLU, and MT-Bench results are included because they report targeted-knowledge suppression and general-capability retention. The paper describes the system as an unlearning approach, but does not apply fine-tuning recovery attacks, activation ablation, quantization, or prompting-only recovery tests. References to prior work's findings are not treated as results from this study.
record.test_reason: AegisLLM is an inference-time guardrail, not weight unlearning. An orchestrator flags WMDP questions and a deflector returns a random letter, so near-chance WMDP accuracy follows from the flag rate (Table 5: 97–99% flagged). The Responder model keeps the knowledge. The paper reports its own system's benchmark performance against baselines and runs no fine-tuning, internal-edit, quantization or prompting recovery attacks on any unlearned model. The RMU/TAR/ELM etc. numbers in Table 2 are a method-comparison table of third-party checkpoints (from Che et al. 2025), with no attack. So no result bears on whether unlearning is shallow or robust.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that AegisLLM, a test-time multi-agent system with DSPy prompt optimization, achieves 'near-perfect unlearning' on WMDP and TOFU, and competitive jailbreak resistance with low false refusal, without retraining. They present it as an alternative to model-modification approaches. They do not test whether suppressed knowledge can be recovered, and the underlying model's weights still contain it.
record.recipe_differences: AegisLLM is a prompt-optimized, inference-time multi-agent routing and response system; it does not modify model weights using gradient ascent, RMU, or the other cited weight-unlearning recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: Prompt optimization changes WMDP outcomes: for Llama-3-8B, Table 5 reports mean WMDP accuracy of 33.2% initially and 26.0% optimized. The paper also reports model-dependent results in Table 5, not extracted here.

fits_no_version.finding: An inference-time multi-agent filter drives Llama-3-8B WMDP accuracy to 24.4/25.4/27.2% (Cyber/Bio/Chem) with MMLU 58.4% and MT-Bench 7.57. This is achieved by flagging queries and answering flagged MCQs at random.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Guardrail or routing systems can mimic unlearning benchmark scores (near-chance WMDP) without removing knowledge from the model.

fits_no_version.finding: In the authors' evaluation, the RMU, RMU-LAT and GradDiff checkpoints on Llama-3-8B leave WMDP-Cyber and WMDP-Chem near base (e.g. RMU Cyber 48.3% vs base 47.2%), while Bio drops toward chance. No attack is applied.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Baseline unlearning effectiveness on WMDP varies by subset in third-party re-evaluations, without any recovery attack.

record.problems: No recovery attacks are tested, so the results cannot establish whether suppressed knowledge is recoverable or removed from weights. Table 2 is reported for Llama-3-8B; uncertainty estimates are not stated.
record.rows_left_out: Table 5 has additional separate initial/optimized WMDP subset and MMLU results for DeepSeek-R1 Distill-Llama-8B, Qwen2.5-72B, and GPT-4o, omitted to keep the record focused on the Llama-3-8B configuration already reported in Table 2 and the Llama optimization comparison. No recovery-attack result is reported elsewhere.

untested.parts: No attack-recovery test on any method; no test of whether knowledge is removed from weights.
No activation ablation or internal analysis.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, language or in-context recovery attempt on WMDP/TOFU suppression. Jailbreak results (StrongREJECT) concern harmful-request refusal, not unlearned knowledge.
AegisLLM is not evaluated against the recovery attacks; no robustness claim is tested.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T2/'tests A' classification is overruled. The system never modifies weights; the Deflector returns random.choice for flagged MCQs. The WMDP result therefore reflects classifier flag rate, not forgetting. The baseline rows are a method-comparison table with no attacks. The Table 5 multi-model results and the TOFU Table 3 results omitted from the rows do not bear on any version either.

versions.untested_parts: The paper reports WMDP targeted-knowledge accuracy and MMLU/MT-Bench retention for its approach and comparison methods. It does not test whether simple attacks recover the knowledge, nor whether the knowledge remains in model weights.
No fine-tuning recovery attack is applied to an unlearned model.
No activation-direction ablation or analysis demonstrating blocked access rather than deletion is reported.
No low-bit quantization recovery test is reported.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, language, or in-context-information recovery test is reported for unlearned knowledge.
The system is evaluated for WMDP suppression, but it is not tested against the recovery attacks named in the claim.

relation.reason: Uses the WMDP benchmark and unlearning baselines without testing whether unlearned knowledge can be recovered. Cites incomplete unlearning only once, as motivation (Cooper et al. 2024), which is too little for 'discusses'.

tranche.reason: Evaluates its own inference-time guardrail on the original's WMDP benchmark, with RMU-family unlearned models as baselines. Reports only its own method's performance and runs no recovery attack, so it is a non-test that uses the original as a tool.

source_check.notes: Near-chance WMDP accuracy comes from the orchestrator flagging 97-99% of WMDP queries (Table 5, optimized) and a Deflector that returns a random option; the Responder model keeps the knowledge. Table 2 and Table 5 give slightly different optimized Llama-3-8B values (Cyber 24.4 vs 24.6, Bio 25.4 vs 26.3). After optimization, 8.3% of MMLU queries are also flagged and answered at random.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: AegisLLM on Llama-3-8B, WMDP and general-capability benchmarks
reader_labels.reason: WMDP accuracy is near the stated chance level across all three subsets while MMLU and MT-Bench remain close to the base-model scores (r41–r45). This supports suppression with capability retention, but not the attack-resistance portion of A.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Comparison methods on Llama-3-8B across WMDP subsets and retention benchmarks
reader_labels.reason: Suppression is uneven across datasets and methods; several target accuracies remain well above chance, and some methods have reduced general-capability scores (r6–r40). No attack-recovery conclusion follows from these evaluations.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: AegisLLM initial versus optimized configuration on Llama-3-8B
reader_labels.reason: The reported mean WMDP accuracy improves from 33.2% to 26.0% with optimization, while MMLU is 59.8% initially and 58.4% after optimization (r46–r49).
